summary: Defines a new access type for the MIME message/external-body type, letting a mail message point at content by URL rather than carrying it. The recipient's program fetches the data from that address.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a MIME message refer to external content using a URL instead of carrying the content itself. The URL is divided into short pieces so it can fit in a message header.

subtitle: A MIME access type that points to external content using a URL.

tldr.problem: MIME external-body parts need a retrieval method, while URL schemes offered retrieval methods without matching MIME access types.
tldr.mechanism: The URL access type stores the URL in a mandatory parameter, split into quoted words no longer than 40 characters.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism supports URLs that retrieve data, while limiting use to a retrieved object matching the declared content type.

today: RFC 2017 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why MIME Needs a URL Access Type
sections.content:
MIME's message/external-body type lets a message point to data instead of including it. Each reference needs an access type that explains how to retrieve the data. RFC 1521 defined several access types, including FTP and MAIL-SERVER.

URLs describe retrieval through many schemes, some without a corresponding access type. The new URL access type is only for URLs that retrieve something; a scheme such as mailto is excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can point to data stored elsewhere. This access type lets the pointer be a URL when the URL retrieves the data.

sections.title: The URL Parameter
sections.content:
The access type is named URL, and its mandatory content-type parameter is also named URL. The phantom body area is left blank. To form the parameter, encode unescaped spaces, control characters, quotes, backslashes, and 8-bit characters, then split the result into words of 40 characters or less.

Place the words, separated by spaces, inside quotation marks. To recover the URL, remove the enclosing quotes and linear whitespace. The RFC says only versions matching the inner message/external-body content type may be retrieved and used.
sections.plainLanguage: The header stores the URL in quoted pieces of up to 40 characters. A reader removes the quotes and spaces to reconstruct it.

sections.title: Security and Integrity
sections.content:
Security concerns are the same as those for URLs used elsewhere; the document defining each URL scheme discusses its specific considerations.

The RFC notes that the Content-MD5 field can check whether the referenced object matches what the message originator intended. It is an integrity check, not a signature service.
sections.plainLanguage: A checksum can help detect whether the retrieved data changed. It does not prove who sent the message.
